power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Previous studies have found that the engagement of domain-general cognitive control facilitates the solution of sentence ambiguities.
This web-based behavioral study investigated the interplay between general cognitive control and linguistic processing.
We examined the interactions between proactive control and processing of English wh-dependencies.

We reasoned that if processing English wh-dependencies engages proactive control, we should observe differences in reaction times and/or accuracy during processing when proactive control is exercised to different extents.

To this end, we manipulated participants' proactive control mode by asking them to perform one of the two variants (less vs. more proactive versions) of the AX-Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), right after which they read English wh-dependency sentences in a self-paced manner.
We also manipulated the gap type (filled vs. control) of the English wh-dependency sentences: filled gaps induce parsing disruptions while control gaps do not.
Our AX-CPT results revealed that participants were in distinct proactive control modes under our manipulation; however, such differences did not modulate the subsequent sentence reading task.
We did observe a filled gap effect at the subject position, in contrast to previous studies.
This suggests that our participants were more proactive than those in prior studies, possibly due to the proactivity manipulation task.
Language processing has been hypothesized to interact with domain-general cognitive control processes, such as memory, attention, and inhibitory control involved in conflict resolution.

Evidence can be found in clinical research of aphasic patients (Brownsett et al., 2014; Schumacher et al., 2019; Stefaniak et al., 2022) and in experimental studies in lab settings (Goral et al., 2011; Gordon et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2021; Hussey et al., 2017; Novick et al., 2014; Traxler et al., 2005).

For instance, Novick et al. (2014) and follow-up studies from their team (Hsu et al., 2021; Hsu & Novick, 2016; Hussey et al., 2017) have consistently found that participants' performance on correctly re-interpreting ambiguous sentences improves after engaging in domain-general cognitive control.

text.text: Prior studies focused on how domain-general cognitive control, specifically, inhibition involved in conflict resolution, can facilitate sentence disambiguation and re-interpretation.
In the current study, we examined the issue from a different perspective by looking at the dynamic interaction between domain-general proactive control and the processing of English wh-dependencies.
In particular, we looked into whether and how exercising domain-general proactive control to different extents can modulate the processing of English whdependencies.
We were specifically interested in knowing whether participants would employ different strategies to process English wh-dependencies when they are biased to be in different proactivity modes.

A preview of the results suggested that we successfully manipulated participants' proactive control mode, but did not find differences between the more and less proactive groups in a subsequent reading task.
In contrast to prior studies on wh-dependencies, we observed a prominent filled gap effect at the subject rather than the object position.
We speculatively ascribed this to our participants being more proactive after being in the proactivity manipulation task.

Wh-dependencies are among the most commonly investigated structures in psycholinguistics and have been extensively investigated across different languages, such as English (Kaan et al., 2000; Phillips et al., 2005; Stowe, 1986; Stowe et al., 1991; Wagers & Phillips, 2014), German (Felser et al., 2003; Fiebach et al., 2001 Fiebach et al., , 2002)), Japanese (Aoshima et al., 2004; Ueno & Kluender, 2009), and Mandarin (Hsiao & Gibson, 2003; Xiang et al., 2014 Xiang et al., , 2015)).

text.text: A wh-dependency sentence typically contains a wh-word that must be associated with another word or syntactic position (a.k.a. argument assigner) to obtain the full interpretation.
In English wh-dependencies, the wh-word usually appears in a clause-initial position and the wh-word and its argument assigner can be adjacent or span multiple words.

For instance, to obtain the full interpretation of the sentence in (1), the language processor must associate the wh-word (who) with the following verb (met/meet) that the wh-word can be an argument of.
Such association can be represented as a filler-gap relation (i.e., the whfiller is filling the empty subject position in (1a), and the object position in (1b)).

A robust finding with respect to the processing of wh-dependencies in English relative clauses is that subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs) are easier to process than objectextracted relative clauses (ORCs); see (2) for examples.
This is reflected by, for instance, faster reading times in SRCs compared to ORCs (e.g., Gibson et al., 2005; Gordon et al., 2001; Staub, 2010; Traxler et al., 2002).

text.text: In the case of English wh-dependencies, it is argued that when our language parser encounters the wh-word, the wh-word will stay active in working memory until it can be integrated with its argument assigner downstream.

Proposals differ as to whether the cost of processing wh-dependencies is due to costs associated with the storage of the wh-word, and/or to interference when the wh-word needs to be retrieved (e.g., Ness & Meltzer-Asscher, 2017 , 2019; Van Dyke, 2007; Vasishth et al., 2019).

text.text: As for storage, the longer the wh-word stays in working memory, the more cognitive costs our language parser incurs for the maintenance (e.g., Chen et al., 2005; Ness & Meltzer-Asscher, 2017 , 2019; Qian & Packard, 2022).

text.text: In terms of retrieval, when more information is introduced before the wh-word can be integrated with its argument assigner, the information will interfere with the wh-word in working memory, resulting in a greater retrieval difficulty of the wh-word for integration (e.g., Van Dyke, 2007; Van Dyke & Lewis, 2003; Van Dyke & McElree, 2006; Vasishth et al., 2019).

text.text: Memory/resource-based models can therefore account for the relatively easier processing of SRCs than ORCs, in that the distance between the wh-word and its argument assigner is shorter in SRCs than in ORCs, thus less cognitively demanding for wh-word retrieval and storage.
Less information will thus be introduced and interfere with the wh-word in SRCs as compared with ORCs.

According to the Active Filler Strategy (AFS) (Frazier & Flores d'Arcais, 1989) and Syntactic Prediction Locality Theory (SPLT) (Gibson, 1998), both examples of memory/resource-based approaches, our language parser postulates potential gaps once it encounters a wh-word in wh-dependencies but always favors the closest gap among all the potential gaps in order to minimize cognitive costs of maintaining the wh-word.

Stowe (1986) conducted a study that probed into this issue and found that parsing was temporarily disrupted at the closest gap when it was unexpectedly filled, which is known as the filled gap effect (at the object position).

text.text: Interestingly, in these studies, parsing disruptions at the subject gap were observed only when the wh-word and the embedded subject were not adjacent to each other and were separated by multiple words (e.g., Alice asked whoi, after the party was over, Kate could drive grandad home to __i.).

The finding of a filled subject gap effect with multipleword interventions between the wh-word and the subject gap can have intriguing theoretical implications for the processing of English wh-dependencies.

text.text: In addition to time, other factors may determine a reader's sensitivity to filled subject and object gaps.
For instance, would individuals who tend to be more pro-active and anticipate more actively be more likely to show filled gap effects than readers who are anticipating less actively?

The present study aims to bias people to be in different proactivity modes, and investigate the effect on processing wh-dependencies, looking both at filled gap effect at the object position, and at subject position.
Cognitive control mediates how one manages thoughts and behaviors to achieve the internal goals.
A widely held assumption is that cognitive control is domain-general and encompasses different underlying mechanisms, such as memory systems, attention, and inhibitory control.
One influential approach is the dual mechanisms of control (DMC) framework, which divides cognitive control into two main mechanisms: proactive control and reactive control (Braver, 2012).
text.formatted: One influential approach is the dual mechanisms of control (DMC) framework, which divides cognitive control into two main mechanisms: proactive control and reactive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Braver, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Proactive control refers to the sustained maintenance of encountered information in working memory.
It is cognitively more demanding as information stays active throughout.
Reactive control, on the other hand, refers to the transient reactivation of previous information in memory upon encountering certain cues.
It is cognitively less demanding as information is activated only when cues are encountered.

These two types of control are not mutually exclusive (Mäki-Marttunen et al., 2019), and individuals can employ them, and shift between them, to different extents in different contexts (Gonthier et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These two types of control are not mutually exclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mäki-Marttunen et al., 2019)</ref>, and individuals can employ them, and shift between them, to different extents in different contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gonthier et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To measure the use and shift between proactive and reactive control, the AX-continuous performance task (AX-CPT) has often been utilized (e.g., Gonthier et al., 2016; Morales et al., 2013 Morales et al., , 2015)).
text.formatted: To measure the use and shift between proactive and reactive control, the AX-continuous performance task (AX-CPT) has often been utilized (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gonthier et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Morales et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Morales et al., , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: A standard AX-CPT is composed of four types of cue-probe pairs: A-X, A-Y, B-X, and B-Y, where A and X are constant letters while B and Y are variables that can be any letter except for A and X. The cue-probe pairs are often separated by 3 intervening letters in a standard AX-CPT.
Participants are instructed to respond to the probe as quickly and accurately as possible via button press.

When cue A is followed by probe X, participants have to press one of the two buttons upon seeing probe X. In other cue-probe pairs (A-Y, B-X, B-Y), participants have to press the other button upon seeing the probe.

The A-X pair usually accounts for most of the trials (e.g., 70% of the total trials) while the rest cue-probe pairs take up and share a relatively small percentage of the trials (e.g., 10% for A-Y, B-X, and B-Y, respectively).

This disproportionate distribution of the A-X pair vs. other cue-probe pairs aims to bias participants to be proactive, as they are likely to anticipate probe X upon seeing cue A under the more frequent occurrence of the AX condition.

Depending on the experimental goal, different variants of the AX-CPT have been used (e.g., changing the distributional proportion of the four conditions, or not having distractor letters between the cue and target) (e.g., Gonthier et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Depending on the experimental goal, different variants of the AX-CPT have been used (e.g., changing the distributional proportion of the four conditions, or not having distractor letters between the cue and target) (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gonthier et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Among the four conditions in the AX-CPT, the AY and BX conditions are particularly important to examine the proactivity and reactivity bias.
If one is proactive, one will be likely to make more errors and/or have longer reaction times (RTs) in the AY condition and fewer errors and/or have shorter RTs in the BX condition.
This is because upon seeing cue A in the AY condition, proactive people will anticipate an upcoming probe X and get ready to respond.
When the probe turns out to be the unexpected Y, proactive people will likely make mistakes and/or show longer reaction times.
Upon seeing cue B in the BX condition, proactive people will already be prepared to make the correct response, resulting in fewer errors and/or shorter RTs in the BX condition.
A reversed pattern is expected if people are reactive (i.e., fewer error and/or shorter RTs in the AY condition and more errors and/or longer RTs in the BX condition).
That is, upon seeing cue A in the AY condition, reactive people will less likely expect the upcoming probe.
They will respond to probe Y when they encounter the probe, thus resulting in fewer mistakes and/or shorter RTs than their proactive counterparts.

However, when reactive people encounter probe X in the BX condition, this probe X will reactivate the cues in both AX and BX conditions, thus causing interference and resulting in more errors and/or longer RTs.
Therefore, in an AX-CPT, performance on the AY and BX conditions is usually examined to evaluate one's proactivity and/or reactivity.

The proactive behavioral index (PBI) is often utilized to quantify one's tendency of being proactive or reactive and is obtained with the following equation, using RTs and/or error rates as inputs: (AY-BX)/(AY+BX) (Gonthier et al., 2016).

text.text: A positive PBI indicates more influence (e.g., more errors, longer reaction times) from the AY condition, thus (more) proactive; a negative PBI, on the other hand, means more influence from the BX condition, thus reactive or less proactive.

text.text: An interesting but rarely explored question, which we address in this study, is whether and how proactivity/reactivity affects the processing of wh-dependencies.
According to the DMC framework, proactive and reactive control operations rely on memory systems to maintain or reactivate encountered information (Braver, 2012).
text.formatted: According to the DMC framework, proactive and reactive control operations rely on memory systems to maintain or reactivate encountered information <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Braver, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These two types of control can also work independently and can be flexibly exercised to different extents in response to different contextual demands (Gonthier et al., 2016; Mäki-Marttunen et al., 2019).

text.text: Based on the prediction-based approach to the processing of English wh-dependencies (e.g., Gibson, 1998), if maintaining a wh-filler and postulating wh-gaps engages domain-general proactive control, then changes in proactive control can potentially modulate such parsing.
text.formatted: Based on the prediction-based approach to the processing of English wh-dependencies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gibson, 1998)</ref>, if maintaining a wh-filler and postulating wh-gaps engages domain-general proactive control, then changes in proactive control can potentially modulate such parsing.

text.text: In the present study, we specifically examine such modulation, if any, from domain-general proactive control to the processing of English wh-dependencies.
Our research question is: can exercising proactive control to different extent modulate the processing of the filled gap in English wh-dependencies?
If so, how?
We will first examine the filled gap effect at the object position.
We will also look at the filled gap at the subject position to further investigate if our proactivity manipulation might play a role.
Our predictions are as follows.

First, concerning the filled object gap effect, when people are biased to be more proactive (by the AX-CPT in the current study), thus employing proactive control to a greater extent, they will be more likely to expect an object gap in processing English wh-dependencies.
When the closest object gap is unexpectedly filled, it will take longer for more proactive people to undo the initial anticipation of this gap and reanalyze the sentence.
On the other hand, when people are biased to be less proactive under experimental manipulation, the expectation of the closest object gap will be reduced.
The unexpectedly filled object gap at the closest gap site will thus be not as much surprising to less proactive people.
They will therefore need less time to recover from the unexpectedness, as compared with their more proactive counterparts.
As for the gap at the subject position, we predict that people in a more proactive mode will elicit a larger filled subject gap effect, compared to their less proactive counterparts.
The same reasoning of the filled object gap applies to the processing of the subject gap.

As the filled subject gap effect is relatively inconsistent in previous studies, if any modulation can be observed, it would add to the literature the potential interactions between parsing strategies and language-specific processing.

The study consisted of two consecutive tasks (i.e., the AX-CPT and sentence reading task) to investigate whether and how domain-general proactive control modulates the processing of English wh-dependencies.
Each participant participated in only one version of the experiment and could do the tasks only once.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the more proactive or the less proactive version of the AX-CPT.
After that, all participants did the same sentence reading task (with list assignments counterbalanced).
Prior to the experiment, participants first read the introduction of the study and gave informed consent on the webpage to agree to participate in the study.
Then, they were asked to read and follow the instructions carefully for the AX-CPT and sentence reading task, which they would perform consecutively in the experiment.

After that, they completed some practice trials (8 practice trials for the AX-CPT, 6 practice trials for the sentence reading task) to familiarize themselves with both tasks before the formal experiment.
During the formal experiment, participants first completed the AX-CPT, right after which they did the sentence reading task.
We did not give instruction reminders between these two tasks so as to facilitate and maximize the intended spillover of the proactivity mode from the AX-CPT onto the reading task.

text.text: A total of 200 cue-probe pairs were created and distributed across the A-X, A-Y, B-X and B-Y conditions for both versions of the AX-CPT (80 for A-X, 20 for A-Y, 20 for B-X, 80 for B-Y).
Note again that A and X were constant letters while B and Y were variable letters that could be any letter except for A and X 1 .
Participants had to respond to the probe as quickly and accurately as possible during the experiment.
When cue A was followed by probe X, participants had to press button J upon seeing the probe.
In other cue-probe combinations (i.e., A-Y, B-X, B-Y), participants had to press button F. The more proactive and less proactive versions of the AX-CPT differed in the following aspects.

In the more proactive version, participants were additionally instructed that cue A was very likely to be followed by probe X, which aimed to bias them to exercise proactive control to a greater extent.

In the less proactive version, additional cue-digit pairs (e.g., A-3, B-6) were introduced in the experiment (20 pairs for A-digit, 20 pairs for B-digit), with the digit randomly selected from 1 to 9.
Participants had to withhold their responses when the probe was a digit and they were not given the additional instructions as in the more proactive version.
The less proactive version was therefore expected to bias participants to exercise proactive control to a less extent.

Example Materials of the AX-CPT Procedure.
In the AX-CPT, a cross was presented for 300 ms, followed by a 500 ms letter cue (of type A or B).
Then, a 3500 ms interstimulus interval (ISI) appeared, which was followed by a 1000 ms probe (of type X or Y, or a digit).

Upon seeing the probe, participants had to respond by pressing a corresponding button on their keyboard (i.e., button J for the A-X condition, button F for the A-Y, B-X, and B-Y conditions) or withhold their response (in the less proactive version) if the probe was a digit.
RTs and (in)correct responses to the probes were recorded.
There was a 1000 ms time-out at the probe frame.
A 1000 ms intertrial interval (ITI) was inserted between trials.
Seven 40-second breaks were evenly distributed in the AX-CPT to avoid exhausting participants; participants could choose to proceed before the 40-second time-out by button-pressing in each break.
After the AX-CPT, a 45-second transitional break was inserted before the sentence reading task.
Analysis.
Analysis of the AX-CPT and reading data was carried out in R version 4.4.3 (R Core Team, 2025) and RStudio (Posit team, 2024).
For the AX-CPT analysis, reaction times and responses to the probes in the AX, AY, BX, and BY conditions were analyzed.
Only trials with correct responses entered the RT analysis.
Unusually short RTs below 100 ms were removed, which accounted for 0.2% of the datapoints.
Since there was a 1000 ms time-out at the probe frame, we did not further cut off slow responses at the probe 2 .
Since the raw RTs had a right-skewed distribution, we carried out a box-cox transformation to better meet the normal distribution assumption.
Specifically, we used the BoxCox() function in the forecast package (Hyndman & Khandakar, 2008) for box-cox transformation with the "loglik" argument.
text.formatted: Specifically, we used the BoxCox() function in the forecast package <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hyndman & Khandakar, 2008)</ref> for box-cox transformation with the "loglik" argument.

text.text: As for the error analysis, all responses to the probes entered the analysis with correct responses coded 0 and incorrect responses coded 1.

In addition to the RT and error analyses, we calculated the proactive behavioral index (PBI) for both RTs and errors to further examine the participants' tendency of proactivity, following (Gonthier et al., 2016).

text.text: Specifically, we utilized the averaged RTs and error rates of the AY and BX conditions for each individual to calculate the PBIs under the equation of (AY-BX)/(AY+BX) 3 .
A positive PBI reflects more difficulty in AY trials, thus a more proactive mode; a negative PBI, on the other hand, reflects more difficulty in BX trials, thus a reactive and/or less proactive mode.

text.text: In (4a), two potential gaps (serving as the object argument) could be postulated upon encountering the wh-word (which): a gap after the verb (hit) vs. the preposition (with).

Procedure.
In the sentence reading task, the self-paced reading paradigm was implemented, in which participants read a sentence word-by-word at a self-paced rate by pressing the space bar.
A sentence contour was presented and a former word would be masked as the sentence was disclosed incrementally word-by-word (non-cumulative moving window display).
Some sentences were followed by a true/false statement verification question that was presented in a full sentence as attention check.
Participants had to press button J (true) or F (false) in response to the questions.
RTs of each word in a sentence and (in)correct responses to the true/false statement verification questions were recorded in the sentence reading task.
Two 40-second breaks were evenly distributed in the sentence reading task and participants could choose to proceed before the 40-second time-out by buttonpressing.
For the analysis of the self-paced reading times, we first removed unusually short and long responses (below 100 ms or above 2000 ms) (Fine & Jaeger, 2016; Prasad & Linzen, 2021).

The present web-based study investigated whether and how exercising domain-general proactive control to different extents could modulate the processing of English whdependencies, focusing on the filled gap site.

While domain-general cognitive control operations have been found to be engaged in language-specific processing in previous studies, we hoped to further contribute to the literature the dynamic modulations between these two distinct domains.
To this end, we created two versions (less proactive vs. more proactive) of the AX-CPT in order to bias participants to exercise proactive control to different extents.
Participants read English wh-dependency sentences right after they performed the AX-CPT.

If the participant's proactivity mode carries over to the sentence reading task, and if processing wh-dependencies shares processes with the AX-CPT, we expected the processing of the wh-dependency, especially with respect to filled gap effects, to be modulated by the version of the prior AX-CPT.
Our expectations were not fully born out based on the results.

First, even though our AX-CPT manipulation was successful in inducing differences in the proactivity mode between the two groups, we failed to find differences between the groups in the sentence reading task.

Second, we did not replicate the filled gap effect at the object position (the window4), but did find an effect at the subject position (the teenager2) following the wh-word/wh-phrase (which1/with which1).

Next, we discuss the findings and implications of the sentence reading task results.
In the AX-CPT, a group difference (less proactive vs. more proactive) that reached statistical significance was observed in both RT and error analyses.
The group exposed to the proactive version of the task had shorter RTs and fewer errors than the group exposed to the less proactive version.
This could not be a speed-accuracy tradeoff as shorter RTs did not lead to more error responses, and vice versa.
Besides, the more proactive group had a larger PBI in both RT and error response analyses.
The results suggested that these two groups indeed behaved differently under our experimental manipulation of two versions of the AX-CPT.
Across the groups, most errors were made in the AY condition, which suggests an overall proactive tendency of the participants.

To recap, our AX-CPT results showed that we successfully biased participants to be in different proactivity modes (less proactive vs. more proactive) under our experimental manipulation, replicating similar patterns in Gonthier et al. (2016).

Previous studies report that young adults tend to be proactive, as compared with young children or older adults (Bugg, 2014; Karayanidis et al., 2011; Kopp et al., 2014; Van Gerven et al., 2016). The participants in our study (18-35 years old) fell into this proactive age range.
Hence, their overall proactive tendency is not surprising.
In the sentence reading task, we did not observe any difference in RTs at the target verb (hit3) as a function of gap type, proactivity group or the interaction between them.
We also did not observe any differences at the filled object gap site (the window4), thus not replicating the filled (object) gap effect (Stowe, 1986).

text.text: However, we did observe a filled subject gap effect that appeared at the earlier word frames of interests.
Specifically, this filled subject gap effect appeared at the embedded subject (the teenager2).

The observed filled subject gap supports the AFS (Frazier & Flores d'Arcais, 1989) and SPLT (Gibson, 1998) which claim that the closest gap (subject gap vs. object gap) is favored to minimize the processing costs.

text.text: We proposed three potential explanations that can account for the observed filled subject gap effect in the present study as well as some possibilities of why no modulations were observed between proactive control operations and the processing of English wh-dependencies.

First, the observed filled subject gap in the present study might result from a generational shift in participants' overall proactivity tendency (less proactive or more proactive), as the filled subject gap effect seems to be observed more often in later time (e.g., Tollan & Palaz, 2021; Wagers & Pendleton, 2016; Yan & Liu, 2021).

text.text: Contemporary young adults may have different sentence processing and/or cognitive control strategies than young adults 20 years ago, perhaps driven by changes in means of communication and communication style, such as brief messages on social media.
Technology has been found to affect cognition in various ways (e.g., Cardoso-Leite et al., 2016; Cudo et al., 2019; Zhang & Xiang, 2023).
text.formatted: Technology has been found to affect cognition in various ways (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Cardoso-Leite et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cudo et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Zhang & Xiang, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To what extent and in what way technology modulates cognitive control and potentially language processing are beyond the scope of present study but is worth exploring for future studies.
Second, it might also be possible that participants' proactivity was boosted after performing the AX-CPT in the present study, regardless of the version of the AX-CPT task they received.
If so, they may have been more likely to anticipate a subject gap during parsing, giving rise to the filled subject gap effect.

This explanation could be tested by conducting a similar study as the current one, but directly comparing the reading results from participants who received the AX-CPT before the reading task with results from those who instead performed a task that does not involve proactive control.
Third, we speculated that the filled subject gap effect might stem from the difference between the argument-related wh-word (which1) and the adjunct-related wh-phrase (with which1).
Specifically, the argument-related which1 can function as the subject of the embedded clause.

Since the subject gap is the closest potential gap in the sentence, encountering an unexpectedly filled subject gap likely disrupted parsing, resulting in the observed filled subject gap effect at the critical noun phrase (the teenager2).
In contrast, the adjunct-related wh-phrase (with which1) can never serve as the subject of the embedded clause.
As a result, no processing disruption would occur when the parser encountered the embedded subject, which is obligatory for grammatical structure formation.
Thus, the filled subject gap effect can be attributed to the distinction between the argument-related wh-word and the adjunct-related wh-phrase.
Furthermore, we speculated that the absence of a filled object gap effect might be influenced by the parsing disruption caused by the filled subject gap.
The filled subject gap (the teenager2) and the filled object gap (the window4) were in close proximity, separated only by the target verb (hit3).
More time might have been required for the parser to detect the filled object gap, especially after recovering from the parsing disruption at the subject gap.
This recovery was reflected in the absence of a spillover effect at the target verb.
Given the short distance between the filled subject and object gaps, the parser may have been unable to register the effect at the object gap, leading to the absence of the filled object gap effect.
Future studies could explore this further by manipulating the distance between the filled subject and object gaps.
As to our failure to observe the modulation of the AX-CPT manipulation on sentence reading, it might be that such modulation effect was too subtle to be easily captured in a behavioral experiment.
An electroencephalography (EEG) study may provide deeper insights into the differences at the neural level (Lin & Kaan, 2025).
text.formatted: An electroencephalography (EEG) study may provide deeper insights into the differences at the neural level <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lin & Kaan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, neural-level modulation has already been observed (Lin & Kaan, 2025).
text.formatted: In fact, neural-level modulation has already been observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lin & Kaan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the effect of our proactivity manipulation may have been short-lasting and may not have carried over to the sentence reading task at the behavioral level.

An interleaved or trial-by-trial experiment design (e.g., Ness et al., 2021) of mixing the AX-CPT and sentence reading trials within a block might be more suitable to test carry-over effects of the cognitive control task onto the reading task.
text.formatted: An interleaved or trial-by-trial experiment design (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Ness et al., 2021)</ref> of mixing the AX-CPT and sentence reading trials within a block might be more suitable to test carry-over effects of the cognitive control task onto the reading task.

text.text: Furthermore, as individuals in early adulthood (18-25 years of age) to late adulthood (~60 years of age) have been found to be inherently proactive (Van Gerven et al., 2016), it might be relatively difficult to suppress their tendency of being proactive (i.e., turning them into being less proactive) and maintain such suppression.
text.formatted: Furthermore, as individuals in early adulthood (18-25 years of age) to late adulthood (~60 years of age) have been found to be inherently proactive <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Van Gerven et al., 2016)</ref>, it might be relatively difficult to suppress their tendency of being proactive (i.e., turning them into being less proactive) and maintain such suppression.

text.text: Even though our proactivity manipulation worked between the two groups in the present study, its effect may not have persisted until the sentence reading task.

Therefore, recruiting participants around the proactivity shifting boundaries (e.g., 14-16 years of age) may help capture such changes and obtain the modulation effects in the behavioral results, if these exist.
Further investigations are thus required in future studies.

To briefly summarize the present study, our goal was to explore whether and how domain-general proactive control could interact with and modulate the language-specific processing of English wh-dependencies, focusing on the filled gap effect at the object position and the filled gap effect at the subject site.
We employed two versions (less proactive, more proactive) of the AX-CPT and successfully biased people to exercise proactive control to different extents.

However, we failed to observe our predicted modulations between proactive control and the processing of English wh-dependencies but the modulations have been observed at the neural level (Lin & Kaan, 2025).
text.formatted: However, we failed to observe our predicted modulations between proactive control and the processing of English wh-dependencies but the modulations have been observed at the neural level <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lin & Kaan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We also failed to find a filled gap effect at the object position, but did observe the filled gap effect at the subject site.
We proposed three potential explanations and suggested possible improvements for the current study design.

Though our predictions were not born out, our study could still contribute to the investigation of the dynamic interaction between domain-general proactive control and language-specific processing of English wh-dependencies.
The observed patterns of the AX-CPT in the present study confirmed that domain-general cognitive control can be fluid and dynamic in response to the external contextual demands.

The filled gap effect at the subject site could particularly serve as motivation for future studies to further explore the interaction between domain-general cognitive control and language-specific processing.
